articles.text:
SHALL IT BE •WAR OK PEACE?

AT the present moment we are at liberty to
say whatever may suggest itself as true and
fitting on the question of the Alabama claims.
In a few days perhaps, should the quarrel

unfortunately go on, public feeling may be-

come so angrily excited that no voice will be
listened to unless in tune with the general
chorus, and has in it a spice of the common
frenzy. We have seen this before; we shall
witness it again if the seething cauldron of
public passion once begins to bubble furiously
up.

And yet we must not forget that we may

be at this moment fronting- dangers of the
gravest kind; that four and twenty hours

may see England and America actively
preparing for a disastrous war ; may
see two countries akin in all noble national
attributes, preparing to imbrue their hands
in each other's blood, not because either
has any interest in the injury or ruin of the
other, but because they have not sense enough
to settle a dispute which every act of outrage
they may commit against each other, will most
assuredly render more difficult of settlement ;
and which in a strict sense of equity never
can be settled either by arbitration or by the
sword in a manner satisfactory to both. That
the Government, and upper and middle classes
of England, acted in a blind and miserably
stupid manner during the American War, is
undeniable. Their sympathy with slavo-
holders was a reproach to them as 'non ;' their
encouragement of an unjustifiable rebellion
against law, was a disgrace to them as citizens,
Whilst their exultation in the anguish of a
people struggling for dear life on battle fields,
made hideous by their vast slaughters, was an
offence not against America only, but against
morality and humanity for which no adequate
atonement ' can be made. And if anything
could be worse than this, the letting out from
our ports of the Alabama and other piratical
cruisers, constituted a culmination in mali-
cious stupidity, inasmuch as it was a des-
truotion of the safety of the seas for
commerce during war, by a people
whose existence as a nation depends on the
inviolability of the great ocean highways of
the world. There is no use hero in alluding
to the offences of the Press. The air is Still
foul from its noisome outpourings, and the
studied humiliation with which it is now
"eating dirt" almost aggravates its past
truculence, as its calmly argued temon-
stranoes at the present moment against the
exaggeration of American demands, servo
Chiefly to remind people of the insulting
bravado with which it at one time rejected
the most moderato of these demands when first
put lomat d.

But when we have admitted all this, and
much more to which it would be needless to
allude, is it not grievous to see that the Go-
vernment and Press of America have now
taken up the playing in this absurd and
miserable game of brag, and seem determined
by their folly to complete the mischief so
stupidly begun by us? It is impossible to
believe that even the most unreasonable per-
son in the United States can hope for compen-
sations arising from these "indirect claims; "
and short of this, what can be required
more than has already been granted ?
It is questionable whether England was
ever at any previous period of her
history humiliated as she has been in
reference to this matter. It cannot be for-
gotten with what a spirit of passionate defiance
we protested against compensation of any
kind, against arbitration, against anything
which went on the supposition of a wrong
done. Now we have only to read Mr. GLAD-
STONE'S statements of last week to understand
how thorough our abasement has been. We,
who protested that we would consider nothing,
apologise for nothing, pay for nothing; we
who asserted over and over again that our
acts must juslify themselves, that our decision
should be the law, have conceded so much,
that were it not for the extravagant additional
concessions we are called upon to make, and
to which we still demur, our faces would be
red with shame and vexation in consequence
of what has been already granted. First, we
have agreed to submit to arbitration in the
face of our loudly expressed determination to
the contrary. And although we tried to
soften our fall by declaring that our giving
way on this point was for the purpose of in-
augurating a new and improved method of set-
tling national disputes, we have cheated nobody
out of a natural belief as to our real motive.
Then again we have agreed to abandon our
counter-claims arising from the Fenian raids
into Canada; and before all, and beyond all
else in importance, we have not only agreed
to pay all direct claims for Alabama and
similar destfuotimp,. but we have consontd to
include in these the cost of the pursuit of these
vessels by the navy of the United States. This,
however humiliating, was politic, and under the
circumstances proper enough to be done. It is
true we have been humbled, but we, deserved
it. We laboured for it and it came to us. A
proud nation, a great nation, a nation rich in
its influencing power, down on its knees before
Europe and the World with scarcely a " rag
left to cover our disgrace," is a spectacle which
our worst enemy might turn from with regret.

Why should America push the matter further
than this ? She has made a Treaty which in
our understanding of it will give her a fair
chance of obtaining everything to which she
is justly entitled. And without adopting
GLIDSTONE'S conclusion as to the completeness
with which any understanding but our, own
is shut out, it may be very safely said that
our interpretation is the most reasonable, and
that it carries in it everything necessary for
the attainment of substantial justice. Why
ask fer more if the intention is not to humil-
iate us ? And what but niischief to America, as
well as to England, can come frota an endea-
vour to force from us what every Englishman
"ith. honeA blood, in his YeillS,wdl reSiSt
the last.? It is quite true that America can
inflict incalculable calamities on England in
case of war; an Empire so o.a:tonatcd as ours

must be open at many points to attack. But
we have our strengths as well as our weak-
nesses; there is abundance of tough fibre in us
yet, and whoever grapples with us in mortal
combat will not escape unscathed from the fray.
But can the statesmen of America be so lost to
every humane and patriotic consideration
as to plunge into a war with us because, as an
essential act of self-respeot, we refuse
to accept treaty conditions which our blunder-
ing negotiators were too stupid to effectually
shut out as unfit to be entertained by the
English nation? And if they do, can we
believe that the working people of America
will blindly and wickedly follow them into a
conflict so unnatural, and so certain to be in-
jurious in its results to all concerned?

If such a war should be entered on, the
principal sufferers on both sides will be those
who live by their labour; and these are the
men who have least cause of offence with
each other—have, in fact, no cause of quarrel
at all. That those half-blind managers of
nations called statesmen, and those scheming
politicians who turn national misfortunes to
personal profit, should promote a war of this
kind is likely enough. Such things have
occurred so frequently that they are just as
likely as not to occur again. Hitherto in this
matter we have trusted to professional nego-
tiators, and they, as we know, have broughrus
to a pass out of which war is the like-
liest issue. . Is it not therefore time
that the people of both countries should
speak for themsolies l Diplomacy has had its
trial, and its failure is dangerously apparent.
Should not every man, therefore, who is
interested in the peace and friendliness of
England and America, raise his voice against
a war which would be fratricidal in all its
acts? We are all of us, members of that
grand Amphietyouie Council, composed of
the consciences of honest, industrious, peace-
loving men; a council, be it remarked, with
sufficient power behind it to enforce its de-
crees; and why not try what can be done
to give practical effect to our sentiments
and convictions on this most pressing and most
important matter for the well-being of both
•countries ? The working men of England
have large claims on the consideration of all
parties in America. They gave them a noble
and valuable support throughout the whole of
their civil war. They sympathised heartily
with them, and suffered deeply through that
sympathy, for them. They, at least, have no
past offence to apologise for, no favour to ask,
no honest suspicion to encounter, no unmanly
fear to prompt them. Why, therefore, should
not the working men of England, whether
in their unions or out of union, at once decide
on sending their own accredited Ambassadors
to the American people, that face to face with
them the cause of peace may be pleaded on
grounds of justice and humanity, in the
interest of both countries, and of all classes
whose aims and objects are legitimate and
patriotic. Such a proceeding might end in
failure, but it is, nevertheless, worth trying.
Half-a-dozen of the cleverest and most trusted
of those who lead our workirg men visiting
the various great towns and cities of America
would be a new feature in the diplomacy of
nations, and Nvould du more tik. bring about a
good understanding between rival States
.than
all the palavering possible between those wiley
go-betweens sent "abroad to lie for the benefit
of their evuutry.' The money neeessary to

carry out such a project well, could easily be
found by the trades societies of the kingdom;
and if the losses through war were estimated,
it would be seen that such an expenditure as
that proposed, would be in reality, a great
economy. If they take it in hand at
all, the working men should find the
whole of the necessary funds themselves.
Such an act of wisdom generously carried out,
would be the first sound practical step in the
direction of a system of international arbi-
tration, carrying with it the promise of per-
manent peace—the first true indication that
the period was arriving when a popular
pacific policy would give fulfilment to those
yearnings for tranquility and progress which
are at present little more than the shadows of
dreams.

LLOYD JONES.

IF France had held Portsmouth for 160
years, if its possession were of the greatest
possible advantage to the French people, if
their title to it had been acquiesced in by our.
selves, and recognised by the rest of Europe,

The mistake consists in not perceiving the dif-

Scientific knowledge can be taught :by

be beneficial; but it will not, indeed it cannot,
supply the teaching of handieraftsmanship,
which needs both physical teaching, and the
training by physical practice, by which alone
can that superiority of manufacturing skill be
established, which will ensure the pro-eminence
of this or any other country as first in the race
of manufacturing excellence.

articles.title: PARKS BILL.
articles.text:
THE PARKS BILL.

THERE is something strangely perverse and
fatalistic about the GLADSTONE Government.
Carried into power by 'a wave of popular
favour, seldom equalled, never surpassed, it
commenced its official career by two brilliant
achievements—that of the Disestablishment of
the Irish State Church, and the Irish Land
Act; but upon these it seals to have spent all
its force.

It is often remarked in domestic life, that
those who can brave its greatest dangers and
overcome its worst difficulties, are the easiest
wrecked by mere trifles. Men, aye, and
women too, who can take arms against a sea
of troubles, and, by opposing, end them, are
frequently borne down by some petty and
insignificant ripple on the stream of life, and
have to acknowledge themselves beaten.
•Such seems likely to be the fate of the
present Government. The meddle and muddle
of the Cab Act is as nothing compared. With
the audacious proposals of Mr. AYRTON in
reference to the Public Parks.

When Mr. GATECORNE HARDY attempted to
" regulate " the Parks, members of the present
Government could give their aid to defeat his
measure, and none more so than the sinister
Mr. AYRTON. But 1u could insult the qtrtmr
in a public meeting (a thing Sir Cullum
DirAcE has never done) when in the ranks of
the" Opposition ; " but to make amends for his
fault he would gag free speech in the Parks
Jest some foolish spluttcrer should say offen-
sive things against Royalty or the present
Cioycrament4

The present attempt to close the Parks
against public meetings is the most barefaced
attempt yet made to take away the right of
public meeting from the people. The bare
idea of some ignorant park-keeper, at a salary
of eighteen or twenty shillings per week,
having the power to interpret the laws relative
to public meetings, and of taking some luck-
less spouter into custody, is so absurd that Nvo
feel inclined to laugh at the suggestion; espe-
cially as Mr. BRUCE is afraid lest policemen
might overstep the mark if they were permit-
ted to interfere with a riotous mob.

The right of free public meeting is too pre-
cious to be thus handed over to irresponsible
persons, such as Park Rangers and Pak
Keepers, and must be maintained at any cost.

But a word to some of our friends; these
meetings have been held too frequently, and
cheaply.

Flaunting flags and banners with red
nightcaps, bands of music, not always musical,
and long processions, especially on a Sunday,
have wearied some of our supporters, nod
made it possible for this atteinpt of Mr
AYILTON, the working man's representative of
the populous Tower Hamlets. Let the right
of meeting in the Parks be kept as a sacred
right, but let it be used wisely and well. That
which was bad in a Conservative Government
to attempt is still worse when done by those
who professed to be shocked by such attacks
on the liberty of the subject, and the audacity
of Mr. Anrrox must be remembered by the
working class voters of the Tower Hamlets at
the next general election.

GEORGE 110 W ELT,.

articles.title: MINES REGULATION BILL.
articles.text:
MINES REGULATION BILL.

The object of this Bill—leave to introduce
which .was given on Monday night—is to protect
children from labour in the mines at too early an
age or for excessive periods, and to bring about a
diminution in the largo number of accidents, as
far as such accidents arise from preventable causes.
This object the Bill seeks to effect by prescribing
general rules for uniform observances in mines,
and requiring special rules to be made for each
mine, all of which rules the owner and agent are
bound under penalties to see carried out. The
guarantees for the enforcement of these rules are a
staff of inspectors, to which it is intended to make
some increase, and an entirely new provision,
whereby every mine is to be placed under the
control of a certified manager, who, as well as the
owner and agent, will be respoqsible for any non-
observance of the Act, through his liability to the
loss of his certificate, as well as to penalties.
The provisions of the Bill which specially'eall
for attention are the following:—
The fill applies to mines of coal, mines of
stratified iron stone, mines of shale, and mines of
fire-clay.

The age for admission to the mines is fixed at
10; boys from 10 to 13 are to be half-timers, and
as such are not to be employed in any one Week
more than three whole days or six half days, the
maximum of a whole day's employment being ten
hours, and that of a half-day's employment six
hours. Such boys are to attend school eight
hours every week without counting attendance at
Sunday school or night school, or school before 8
in the morning, or any attendance in excess of
three hours at a time or five hours in a day.
Lads from 13 to 16 are restricted to 56 hours of
labour per week. For all under 16 an interval of
rest of 12 hours is .secured between each day's
employment, except between Friday and Saturday,
when an interval of eight hours will be per-
missible, in Order that the boys and lads may, by
beginning work earlier on Saturday morning, be
able to leave earlier in the day, and so enjoy the
Saturday half-holiday. _ _

Sufficient intervals for meals are secured when-
ever the period of employment exceeds five hours.
The person in charge of an engine for raising or
lowering miners is required to be 18 years of age.
If the engine is worked by a horse, the person
directing, the driver, and not the driver him,self, is,
as under the existing enactment, to be deemed to
be the person in charge of the engine, but the
driver is required to be 12 years of age. Where
wages are paid according to the quantity of mate-
rial wrought, payment is to be made exclusively
by weight, save in exceptional cases, where, from
local exigencies,' measuring or gauging may be
sanctioned by special 'exemption from the Se-
cretary of State. The use of the standard weights
is to be enforced to the exclusion of any conven-
tional system.
Double shafts are required, and the communi-
cation between the two shafts is to be throughout
not loss than 4ft. wide and aft. high. The
enforcement of this enactment is, in the case of
such mines as are not now required to have two
shafts, to be postponed to January 1, 1875, and
the power is reserved to the Secretary of State to
exempt fire-olay mines, wherever a second shaft
seems unnecessary. In accordance with the pre-
cedent of the Merchant Shipping Acts, esch mine
is to be under the control of a manager, to be
appointed by the owner, who may appoint either
himself or Some other person. But the manager
must be certificated. A certificate is only to be
obtained by a person who passes an examination
conducted by examiners appointed by the Se-
cretary of State, and gives satisfactory evidence of
his sobriety, experience, ability, and general good
conduct. It is intended that this examination
should be conducted locally, and be of a thoroughly
practical character.

To this rule, however, an exception is made in
favour of those who were in the position of
myiagers on the Ist of Jannary, 1872, nnd have
continued to be so up to the passing of the Act.
Such persons will be permitted to take out certifi-
cates 'without passing any examination.

If at any time an inspector of a district reports
that an inquiry is expedient to ascertain whether
U. manager is not, by reason of incompetence,
drunkenness, or gross negligence, unfit to discharge
Ins duties, the Secretary of State may direct a
formal public investigation to be conducted by a
court to be specially constituted for the purpose,

and the Court will have power to suspend or
cancel the certificate of the manager, power of
remis-ion being reseryed to the Secretary of State,

The general rules contained in the 13111 of last
session are amended and additions are made to
them. If any person contravenes or fails to com-
ply with any general or special rule, such person,
and also the owner, agent, and manager, are each
to be criminally liable; but each may exonerate
himself by proving that he took all reasonable
moans to prevent such contravention or non-
compliance.
The principal amendments to the general rules
as contained in the Bill of last session are :-1,
That in the first general rule, which requires
ventilation sufficient to render the mines safe under
ordinary circumstances, the words "under ordi-
nary circumstances " are
.expunged ; 2, that
further restrictions upon the use of powder in
fiery mines are introduced; 3, that guiding and
signalling machinery are to be provided in deep
shafts; 4, that provision is to be made to prevent
the rope slipping either on or off the drum.
The principal additions to the general rules are
the following :—The owner, agent, and manager
of the mine are required to see to the propping of
the roof and sides of the working places, as well
as of the roadways; to cause an inspection to be
had of the ventilation before workers are admitted
to the mine, and of the mine generally every day;
to withdraw the workmen in case the mine be
found in a dangerous condition; to allow the
workmen once a month to inspect and report upon
the mine. To appoint in each mine a station
or stations beyond which workmen are not to go
without special authority; to allow the workmen
the option of using either the downcast or upcast
shaft where each is available for ascending or
descending, and to have a man in attendance to
raise any workman who is in the mine. New
special rules are to be required in the case of each
mine after passing the Act.
With regard to abandoned mines the side en-
trances are to be fenced as well as the top of the
pit shaft, and the maps to be deposited are to be
copies of the most recent working maps.
_ _

The Metalliferous Mines Bill follows the Coal
Minos Bill in its provisions as to the employment
of boys and lads under 16, but tho provision re-
quiring that every mine should ,be placed under
a certified manager is not incorporated, being
deemed unnecessary.
The general rules are for the most part the same
as those contained in the Metalliferous Mines
Bill of hat session, the most important additions
being the general rules, which relate to the fol-
lowing matters :—The restriction upon the use of
powder, the placing of ladders and supplying the
ladder round with sollars at certain intervals, and
the separation in the shaft of the ladders or man-
engine from the machinery for raising the
minerals. From some of the provisions of the
Bill, mines are exempted wherein not more than
12 persons are employed underground; and, in
consideration of the hodeycombed character of
some Of the mining districts, the general enact-
ment requiring all abandoned, shafts to be fenced
is qualified by certain limitations; but no shaft is
to be left unprotected which the inspector of the
district requires to be fenced.

articles.title: LATE TRADES CONGRESS AND
articles.text:
THE LATE TRADES CONGRESS AND

THE FACTOR-Sr ACTS.

According to the decision of the late Trades
Unions Congress, the Secretary was instructed to
mernorialise the Home Secretary to appoint an
additional number of inspectors to enforce the pro-
visions of the Faotories Extension and Woticshops
Regulation Acts. The following memorial was
forwarded to Mr. Bruce, and the accompanying
reply received; and also, at the same time, an
acknowledgment of the receipt of the petition
from the Congress on the Mines Regulation Bill.
"To the Right Honorable; Henry Austin Bruce,
" M.P., Her Majesty's Home Seerooary. ,

,
"The humble memorial of the delegates form-
ing the Trades Union Congress, held at Notting-
ham during the week ending:January 13th, 1872,
and representing directly upwards of three hun-
dred thousand members, shwa!'—
" That your memorialists, having taken into
consideration the beneficial effects that have accrued
from the Factories Extension and Workshops Re-
gulation Amendment Acts, believe that still
greater benefits would be derived by the appoint-
ment of an additional number of efficient inspec-
tors to enforce the provisions of the said Acts, the
present number being wholly inadequate to a proper
discharge of their duties, partly from the extensive
area of the districts assigned to them, and also
from the necessary requirements of the regula-
tions, the appearance of an inspector in any
factory or workshop being of Ipre occurrence.
From the rapid extension of factories andawork-

shops it is also of vast importance that the number
of inspectors should be further increased without
delay, so as to make evasions of the law fewer in
future than at the present time.
"We therefore wish, through you, Sir, humbly,
but earnestly, to memorialise Her Majesty's
Government to carry out the views entertained
by us on behalf of the Congress.
" WILLI.tst HlcKitio, Secretary.

[REPLY.]

"Whitehall, February 9th, 1872,

"SIR,—I am directed by Mr. Secretary Bruce
to acknowledge the receipt of the memorial of the
Nottingham Trades Unions Congress, suggesting
the appointment of an additional number of in-
spectors to enforce the provision of the Factories
Extension and Workshops Regulation Acts, and I
am to acquaint you that an increase has been
made in the staff of the Factory Department,
which it is believed will be sufficient for the pur-
poso.—l am, Sir, your obedient servant,

"A. J. 0. lannELL.
"Mr. Win. Ricking, Secretary to the Trades
Unions Congress, Nottingham."

articles.title: TEE WORKING MEN OP COVENTRY AND THE RELATIONS BETWEEN CAPITAL AND LABOUR.
articles.text:
TEE WORKING MEN OP COVENTRY
AND THE RELATIONS BETWEEN
CAPITAL AND LABOUR.

On Monday evening last, Mr. George Potter, of
London, addressed a crowded meeting of working
men in St. Mary's Hall, on the above subject.
The Mayor (W. 11. Hill, Esq.) presided, and there
were also present, Rev. E. IL Dell, Aldermen
Marriott and -Streetly, and Councillors C. J. Hill,
T. Hill, J. Parish, J. E. Banks, and J. Loudon,
and Messrs. W. Taunton, I. W. Lewis, E. Goode,
J. Dadley, and the leading men of the various
trades.

The Mayor, in introducing the lecturer, said:"
Gentlemen, a deputation from the Joiners' Mao-
ciation waited upon Me, and, at their request, I
consented to preside to-night. Until this evening
Mr. Potter was an entire stranger to me, but I
cannot say I am entirely a stranger to his writings.
I have read several of his addresses with very
great pleasure. How he may intend to treat the
subject to-night of course 1 cannot tell, but I
have no doubt we shall find that he Will treat it
in a way that will tend to bring together both
classes—capitalists and working men. Of course
we may expect that he will treat it principally
from a working man's point of view, but this may
be done, I consider, quite in strict justice towards
both classes. (Hear, hear.) And when one class
presents its claim to the other in a reasonable and
a moderate form, it is sure to deserve 'the respectful
attentionof the other, and by that means you will
generally find the result will be that strikes will
be avoided and disputes easily settled. This is
not a political question; gentlemen, it is a social
one, and on that account I consented to occupy
the chair to-night. I thought it was quite right
that the working classes should have an oppor-
tunity of hearing one of their best advocates, and
I may say an old Coveitry apprentice and work-
Man. (Cheers.) It was quite right, I thought,
that they should have an opportunity of hearing
such a person discuss the merits of that great ques-
tion of the day—the connection between capital and
labour. * (Hear, hear.) I am glad to say to you;
and you 'all find it to be true, that trade is a great
deal better than it has been in Coventry for a long
time past. I hope it may long continue. I sincerely
hope that those complications which are arising in
connection with the American affair will be brought
to a speedy and peaceful settlement; otherwise we
may fear that the industry of this country will be
to a considerable extent interfered with. I see in the
daily paper of this morning that the value of railway
property, setting aside any other class of property,
has depreciated within the last week, in conse-
quence of this American affair, to the value at least
of twenty millions of moner. So that if indirect'
claims are to be presented on the part of America,
and this may go on for any length of time, we
shall very soon have a long list of indirect claims
to present, I think, to them. I am glad to know
now that the working man, while trade remains as
it is, • is better paid—is not only better rewarded,
but has more time in his hands for relaxatlon and
self-improvement. And I sincerely hope that the
working classes generally will make the best use
of these opportunities ; that they will encourage
and promote industrious habits, and thereby make
their homes happy and coniAntable. (Cheers.)
I shall be glad to find that intemperate habits are
giving way to temperate habits, for by that means
they will find greater comforts in every respect.
A habit of study and reading will then be
formed, and the bent:lit of that will soon be
realised. They e ill then value the education
of their children, and we shall find that the
compulsory clause—to compel their children to

attend school—will he very little required. Let
each of us, my friends, do our part to tarry out, or
help to carry out, such a good work as that which is
now going on in our country—l mean the pro-
ITIQUOU of the education of. the children of the
working classes. I will not detain you any longer,
gentlemen. You arc all desirous to bear Mr.,
Potter's lecture, I know, and I beg now that you
will give him a patient and quiet hearing. Let us
all listen as those who want to get as much know-
ledge as we can. (Loud cheering.)
Mr. Potter, who was most enthusiastically re-
ceived, then gave an interesting address upon the
subjects of the evening, which appeared to give
general satisfaction,

After which Mr. Walker, carpenter, proposed,
and Mr. Owen,brieklayer, seconded, a vote of thanks
to Mr. Potter, which was carried by acclamation.
- •
Mr. Potter, In rasing to respond, was heartily
cheered. Ile said: Mr. Mayor and Gentlemen,—l
am very much obliged to you for your vote of
thanks. I hope and trust that you will give me
credit of haviug pure and 'earnest. intentions in
being present to-night. I have not been for many
years in Coventry. I was apprenticed in Coven-
try, and I worked here at my trade for several
years, and, therefore, when I come to this town, I
come almost, as it were, to my native place.
(Cheers.) I dare say many of you, as it is eighteen
years ago, have forgotten the circumstances, but
still I feel to-night pleased to think -that I should
be able, as one of yourselves, to occupy this posi-
tion humbly as I do to-night. I have endeavoured
since I have been called to public life to 'put the
working men's case in as temperate, fair, and
honest a manner as r possibly could, and believe
it is that which has gained for me some consider-
able 'degree of respect and appreciation on the part
of my fellow working men. (Applause.) I think
that it is our bounden duty to try to do what' we
can for the benefit of our fellow men. We are in-
debted,: Mr. Chairman, as you know, for many.. po-
litical and social rights to our forefathers. Well, now
we enjoy those rights it is our duty to confer them
upon our posterity, increased if we can—" to leave
the world better than we found it." (Hear, hear)
The duty of every man, therefore, though we
can't all be speakers and writers, though we can't
all be employars, and though we can't all be well
off, we can all in our limited circle exercise an
influence for good—an influence of a progressive
character, an influence of leading on, lifting up,
not treading doe n, building up, not pulling down,.
thinking as we act, and consummating our nets by,
every good judgment we possess. (Hear, hear.)
I ion exceedingly thankful, working-mon and
gentlemen, that you have listened to me to-night
in the manner you have. It is a difficult thing to
stand up in an audience like this, and propound
questions of such immense importance. The
responsibility is groat, and white we try to
do it we are glad that we have your
appreciation, and we ask you to reject everything
that you think wrong or unworthy, and ponder
and mature on all that you think is good and right.
(Cheers.) Now, I have great pleasure in pro-
posing that the best thanks of this meeting he
given to the Mayor for the use of dila raom, and
for his kindly presiding over us to-niuht. (Cheers.)
You know the Mayor better than I do. I have not
met him before this evening, and I have not had
many Minutes' conversation with him ; Therefore I
know very little about his public character. That
he is interested in the welfsre of woiking men is
manifested by his appearance hero ta-night at our
meeting. (Cheers.) The Mayor felt that the
working men wished to hear an address upon this
subject, and they waited upon him, and he con-
ceded their request and then kindly consented to
preside, and we are, greatly indebted to him fir it.
Now, working men, this is another sign of the
times. When the Trades' Unions hal their Con-
gress at Nottingham last month, we had a now
feature thrown into our deliberations. The
Mayor of Nottingham invited .every dele-
gate to a banquet given in the Town Hall. The.
members of Parliament of that borough, with
Ur. Samuel Morley, who. has a great interest in
Nottingham, invited the de!ogates to breakfast,
and there were clergymen of the Chui di of Eng-
land, and Dissenting ministers, and large em-
ployers, and Ochincillors, and the Mayor of the
Bordugh, all inviting delegates representing Trades'
Unions. (Loud cheers.) Now these are signs of
the times which we accept and recognize, and we
must see to it, that if they are desirous to help us'
in every good and legitimate work, we must do ai
we can to advance ourselves. 13e prepared to help
yourselves. Recognise every help, or any help
that comes from outside, itnd I am sure 'that you
with me to-night fully thank the Mayor for his
kindness in presiding, and for the use of this room.
In order to testify this, you who are of that
opinion will hold up both hands.
The Mayor, who was received with loud cheers,
briefly acknowledged the vote of thanks, and the
meeting Separated. •

[We have taken this report from the Coventry
/iota of wodnudey, in which. also appears A full
report of Mr. Potter's address.]

After the meeting, Mr. Potter met a large num-
ber of the vatious trades at the Joiners' Soviety
House, at which it was resolved that he should he
invited to vitit Coventry again on an early day for
the purposa oe addressing the various trades on,
social and ',Withal subjects.

articles.title: WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE FOR PROMOTING THE
articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
FOR PROMOTING THE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO THE WORKING CLASSES OP GREAT BRITAIN.

FELLOW WORKMEN,—
The Working Men's Committee has been, formed
in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miall to
the judgment of the House of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature to
apply the principle of that measure to the rest of
the United Kingdom. lie was met with the objec-
tion that the case of Ireland was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendowment and disestablishraent
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was not yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Miall, that he must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.

This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted ; and the Society for the Liberation
of Religion from State-Patronage and Control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro-
nounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has beenfelt that, afterthe broad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain from
a declaration of their honest and deliberate senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall, and the great party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
leader of the Liberal party in the House of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Mon, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested byMr. Gladstone, as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the Die-
endowment and Disestablishment of the State.
Church in Britain, as in Ireland; but also,
and perhaps especially, with a .view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General Election, whensoever that may take
place. The House of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, doss not embody a faithful and com-
plete representation of the whole• people; and,
without taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists In the election of a House of Commons,
each member of which has been returned with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.
These, then, are the circumstances unaer which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting the
Separation of Church 'and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.

The views of the Committee may be thus eon-
sisely stated—.

1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker.

2. They are of opinion that, sinoe the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been diSestablished, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the United
Kingdom

3. They are persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has utterly
failed to accomplish the task for which it was
established; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects which churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.

4. The State-Church of England has failed as
'manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Irish People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Protestantism of the then
State-Church, the great majority of the 13ritish
People are either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish.
meat.

5. The immense revenues ,of the English and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; because
those revenues, though the common property
of the whole nation, are distributed among the
religious teachers of half, or less than half, of the
people. Enormous and disproportionate salaries

FEn. 17, 1872.

and emoluments are paid to Bishops and other
Dignitaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by die parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the few cat
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations.

6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment la
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. Jealous
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that of
the Establishment in which they have so strong a
vested interest. Hence, in every agitation of 3
political or social character, they are always on
one side and the People on the other.
7. The Establishment is a source of national
weakness, because it divides the nation into two
hostile parties. It prevents good men uniting, as
they otherwise might unite, in works of philafl.
thropy and in movements for social reform. It
thus carries a mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affairs of life.

Such are the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the serious consideration
of their feltbw workmen throughout the country.
In order to ascertain and give effect to their views,
Branch Committee d will be formed, and meetings
held, in all the large towns. It is hoped, and believed,
that the practical result will be that, after this
great question has been submitted to the electors,
when it is next debated in the House of Commonse
Mr. Miall will be in a position to give to Aft'
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisive
answer.—We are, on behalf of the Working
Men's Committee, Yours faithfully,
• GEORGE HOWELL (Chairman).
DAINIRL GUILE (Treasurer).
GKORGE POTTEII (Secretary)..
10, Bolt Court, Fleet-street, London, E.C.

SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 17, 1872.

THE MINES REGULATION BILL.

--
TEE Regulation of Mines Bill, a summary
of which we give in another column, has bee°.
brought into Parliament, and contains several
changes, and Mr. BRUCE professes to hav°
considered the suggestions of the working
miners. With respect to boys, it is the saint)
as last year's Bill, with one exception. 1$
previous Bills the age for admission was tell,
but this adopts the principle of the FactorY
Act. Last year it was proposed that boys of
that ago should only be allowed to work
limited number of hours, but now it is in-
tended to adopt the six half-days. Witb
regard to children under thirteen, there lo $
change from twelve' to ten hours. The edum

cation provisions aro practically unaltered,
also the clauses respecting payment of wages.
This subject will be dealt with in the Bill
relating to the Truck Act. A uniform system
of weighing coal has much to recommend it;
but would put proprietors to great expense.
The Bill, therefore, proposes to adopt the
system of weighing; but reserving to the
Secretary of State to sanction the other system.
There is to be a uniform weight. When two
shafts are necessary, the communications be-
tween are ta be four feet wide, and three feet
high. With regard to accidents, the
average of deaths in the year amounts
to one thousand, besides other accidents.
The average deaths caused by explosions is
about one-fourth of the whole. Last year the
deaths were 991, and only 185 due to explosions.
The greater part arose from carelessness of the
men and want of the discipline of the managers.
Last year 441 deaths and numerous accidents
occurred from the falling of masses of stone.
If the collieries were properly overlooked,
these accidents would not have taken place.

It is the opinion of the inspectors that if
greater responsibility were thrown on managers
a great saving of life would be effected. In a
colliery a manager is to be appointed by the
owner and registered. At present any breach
of duty is punishable by fine invariably paid
by the master, and no neglect short of death is
otherwise punishable Wherever a manager is
found, guilty by a coroner's jury, the bill is
invariably thrown out by the grand jury, and
there is no example of conviction of
a manager, however gross and patent his
negligence. The manager will now be vested
with real responsibility. Every manager not
a manager on the Ist of January, 1872, will
be subject to examination. Existing managers
will be required to have a eertlicate. The
examination will be strictly practical. The
owner will be responsible for selecting a
manager of sobriety, experience, ability, and
general good conduct. Managers will be
liable to have certificates cancelled or sus-
pended. Tho examining board will be con-
stituted by the Secretary of State. It will be
a local board, composed generally of an
inspector and a person practically acquainted
With mining. With regard to the roofs and
sidings of roadways and working places,
obligations are thrown on the owner
and manager to keep them in a proper
condition.

Another rule, introduced for the first
time, has reference to gunpowder. As
'a general rule, no powder will be taken
into a pit except in cartridges. Under no plea
or shape whatever will powder be allowed to
be used for blasting coal, but it may be used in
those mines for blasting rook, under the direc-
tion of a competent person. The amendment
of the member for Ayrshire will be adopted
With regard to ventilation. There arc provi-
sions for inspecting mines every twenty-four
hours to see if there is any appearance of
danger, to provide for the due warning of the
Men, and one in particular which empowers
the men to appoint two of their number to
inspect and examine every part of the mine
once a month. There is also a provision for
the more efficient covering of the men when
ascending or descending, and for promptly
bringing men to the surface.
When the recommendation of the Select
Committee appeared to provide for the efficient
ventilation of the mine, the words used were
that the owners should be bound to apply
Proper ventilation to render the mine safe
under ordinary circumstances, and it was
objected to those words that they placed the
owners in a different position to any one else,
because it casts on them the duty of proving
a negative. This, Mr. Damn says, is really
unavoidable, and it will be open to the owners
to prove that the accident occurred from a
sudden fall of rook, or from some mischievous
person removing something. The difficulty is
that, when an accident occurs every trace of the
cause is destroyed, and there are no means of
Proving that the mine was properly ventilated.
In his view it should be for the employers to
show that the ventilation was sufficient in the
ordinary state of the mine; and, if they
could do that it would be at once assumed
that the accident was due to some temporary
cause, such as all collieries aro subj cot to.

A largo proportion of accidents arise from
the roadways. In order to obviate that, the
Bill contains a provision that the tramways be
placed all on the same side, because it fre-
quently occurs that an accident happens in
crossing the road. The men wanted all the
mines, once in every quarter, to be thoroughly
inspected by the Government inspectors, and
a responsible Minister to control them. That,
says Mr. BRUCE, is opposed to the policy of
Parliament, and would not really be to the
interest of the men. Their safety depends,
not on a thorough quarterly inspection, but
on a thorough daily inspection, which this
Bill will provide, and which will very much
increase the responsibility of the managers.
Besides which, the Bill will enable them to
control the inspection infinitely better than
by any Government machinery. At the same
time, Mr. BRUCE does not say that the number
of inspectors is sufficient; for, in point of fact,
they are utterly insufficient to make such an
inspection as the Bill proposes. Some increase
in the inspectors will bo made, such as the
increasing number of the collieries demands,
but the Government are altogether opposed to
transfer the responsibility of the colliery
owners and managers to the State.

. REPEAL OF THE CONTAGIOUS
DISEASES ACT.
THE Home Secretary has introduced his
Bill for the repeal of the Contagious Diseases
Acts, and for the institution of certain regu-
lations bearing upon the same subjects. He
began by describing the motive and effort of
previous legislation with a particularity in
which it would be unpleasant, and is needless,
to follow him. Suffice it, that, without any
strain put upon them, his words admitted the
arbitrary nature of the arrests of women and
the conversions of pretended hospitals into
real prisons. The Lords, he made it appear,
were so charmed with the invention that their
committee were the first to propose the ex-
tension of the method from the two military
services to the civilian population generally.
"There was no doubt," said Mr. BRUCE,
"that this led to the agitation which had
since raged throughout the length and breadth
of tho eountry." On that agitation, never-
theless, the Right Ronourable gentleman
boldly charges "monstrous perversion and
exaggeration," and still claims for the doomed
statutes that they have worked in a most
satisfactory manner.
The weakness of the moral and religious
public has proved too strong for the HOME
SECRETARY and the sneering doctors who
gained the ascendancy over him. A Commis-
sion of inquiry was issued, which reported in
the teeth of the conclusion that the Home
Office and its medical staff had come to. The
minority of seven, led by Sir Jorm PA.KING-
TON, were unable to convince their colleagues
that the condemned legislation was the only
thing that could either renovate the army and
the navy, or save the country. In his analy-
sis of the evidence, Mr. BRUCE made one
strong claim as to the effects produced, which
every father and mother will rejoice to find
Confirmed by actual experience; we refer to
the asserted "almost entire " suppression of
juvenile prostitution.
The point on which the Government, after
the inquiry, felt constrained to give way before
the outset of public opinion was, the imprac-
ticability of maintaining such laws for the
military service in the midst of civilians.
They were of opinion that it was impossible to
maintain in certain limited districts and
among a largo civil population a system not
capable of being extended to other parts of
the country. The system of periodical and
compulsory examinations could not be made
the basis of general legislation. These Acts,
it was said, had been carried by surprise but
it was not the fault of the Government that
they did not receive discussion.lThe subjects
were not such as to invite discussion and the
consequence was that this very stringent legis-
lation passed through the House almost without
notice. Novel principles were introduced
among a population utterly unprepared for
their application. Let Mr. BRUCE'S explana-
tion of the matter go for what it may be
thought worth. The great thing is, that these
nasty Acts arc to be witslitd out of the statuto

book which they had been permitted to
defile.

It must needs be edifying to hear the Minis-
ter who defended the Acts as long as he could
and who even now, strains every point to
make their repeal matter for regret, setting
up for the office of grand patron and pro-
tector of the virtue and innocence of young
persons of the female sex. But first, he
proposes to deal with women of some advanced

years by an extension and amendment of the
Vagrants Act, which, for like purposes, is to
be applied to Scotland and Ireland. The now
legislation is intended to clear the streets of
the lowest and most impudent clasi of
strumpets. Such of them as, on arrest, are
found diseased, will be imprisoned, not only for
the term specified, but till cured. These re-
gulations will apply not merely to vagrant
prostitutes, but to all women committed by
magistrates, ascertained to be on the town.
For the present, however, the enactments will
stop at this point, and not embrace women
sentenced pursuant to the verdicts of juries.

The surgeon will report the person suffering
from disease. The report will be sent by the
gaoler to a justice of the peace, who will make
an order for detention; and a woman detained
after term of sentence expired may, by order
of the justice, be removed to a certified
hospital. But, if not sooner cured, her deten-

tion will not exceed nine months. The chief
medical officer of the prison infirmary,or certified
hospital, will be required each month toltrans-

mit a certificate that further detention is
necessary. The justice will have power to
discharge a woman from the prison infirmary
or certified hospital, though not cured, if satis-
fied she intends to lead a moral life.

For the protection of women, it is proposed
to extend from ten to twelve years, the age
within which the abuse of a girl is punishable
with penal servitude for life, and from twelve
to fourteen, the age with respect to which
similar misconduct entails ten years' penal
servitude. To obtain possession by false pre-
tences of a girl under twenty-one is at present
punishable by imprisonment for two years.
The same punishment is to apply in any case,
irrespective of age. He asked the support of
the House in measures of the utmost severity
against those who knowingly harbour children
for immoral purposes. He proposed to make

the harbouring of children under sixteen
punishable with six months' imprisonment
summarily before a magistrate, or, on an in-
dictment, with two years, with or without
hard labour, at the discretion of the judge.
He proposed also that the parochial authorities
might prosecute keepers of disorderly houses,
instead of the initiative being taken by two
ratepayers; and to make the landlord liable
for keeping a disorderly house, if he knew it,
although not resident and taking no part in
the management. He proposed to give the
power summarily to terminate the holding of
a disorderly house, whatever the lease might
be. Common lodging-houses would be de-
prived of their licence, and the keepers sub-
ject to punishment if they knowingly per-
mitted disorderly persons to frequent them.
The greater part of these provisions were
founded upon the recommendations of the
Commissioners, and some suggested by an ex-
amination of the general law. Mr. BRUCE
hopes to prevent the corruption of young
persons, and provide guarantees for public
order. It might be asked why not extend this
legislation to the whole country without inter-
fering with Acts admittedly doing much good?
But it was impossible to maintain laws which
had not the sanction of publics opinion. There
was no wiser maxim than that of Burke, that !
legislation should not force but follow opinion.
At present opinion had been forced rather than
followed. The reserve and delicacy for which
the female part of our population was so dis-
tinguished had been broken through, and a
renewal of the agitation would produce dis-
astrous results. If these evils were to be
cured or greatly diminished, it could only be
done by voluntary agency—by the efforts and
zeal of benevolent persons.
Well, we will not twit the HOME SECRE-
TARY with this abandonment of Acts which
he still thinks excellent. Nor will we trouble
ourselves to set in array against his band of.
army and navy doctors the ample testimony

of medical men of the highest respectability
all over the country. We are thankful for the
partial victory which; we have achieved, and
must rely upon our Parliamentary leaders for
taking care that the snakes do not lie concealed
in the fair and fresh-looking verdure of the new
Bill. Dr. B HEWER is of opinion that the doomed
acts have done more for the good of the people
that the united efforts of the whole religious
world, and Sir Jonpr PAKINGTOM upbraids Mr.
BnucE with pursuing a timid and unworthy
course. Sir J. ELPIIINSTONE taunts him with
cowardice. Language like this should call
forth all our vigilance, lest, by some secret
contrivanco, we be cheated of our victory.
We have the declaration of Mr. ltyLA,Nns as '
one of the Commissioners, that although they
entered on the inquiry with [a large majority
in favour of the Acts as they stood, they came
to a conclusion entirely different, on the
ground, no doubt, that the:good effects pro-
duced might be due to other causes in opera-
tion concurrently with the Acts to which the
effects were specifically attributed. From the
other side of the House, Mr. HENLEY, a man
as sagacious as he is honest, contends for it as
an undoubted fact, derived from the reports of
Commissioners and Committees, that quite as
many, if not more, fallen women are reclaimed
in towns in which tho Act is not in operation
as in those in ;which it is. Finally, Mr. Ox-
WAX stands up for those praiseworthy women
who devoted their energies to obtain the
repeal of Acts degrading to their sex. He
represents a borough in which the Acts are in

operation, and he totally differs as to their
effect. They must remember they are legis-
lating for women who have no opportunity of
making themselves heard except through the

disinterested efforts of those of their own sex
who have taken up their cause. When the

Government are blamed for this new measure,
he asks Whether no account is to be taken of
the feelings of the country? It is undeni-

able, he maintains, that the working classes

to a man are in favour of the repeal. Yes,
and we hold ourselves prepared, if necessary,
to make a second demonstration of the fact.

articles.title: lIONIE RULE IN IRELAND.
articles.text:
lIONIE RULE IN IRELAND.

WHETHER there is any sound political
meaning in the question of Home Rule or not,
it is quite clear that it has taken possession of
the minds of many people in Ireland.
It may be that those in favour of it are foolish
persons, or turbulent and disloyal fanatics,
priest-led dupes, or designing agitators. It
is not difficult to settle a question to our own
satisfaction, by impugning the motives or
disparaging the characters of those by whom
we are opposed. This, however, is a method
of settlement which seldom answers; and,
applied to Ireland in the present instance, it
does not appear very likely to meet with much
success. That Irish politicians are wrong-
headed, and therefore most difficult to deal with,
is very likely true enough; and that their idea
of Home Rule may mean repeal of the Union,
and ultimately separation, need not be denied.
Still, much can be said in favour of Home
Rule fairly stated and rightly understood. It
is not possible to deny that much of the busi-
ness now done in the British Parliament,
especially local business, is done in a dilatory,
slovenly, and expensive manner, and at hall-
nitc trouble and vexation, and great cost, to
those who are interested in it. Without having
the least desire to give countenance to chimeras,
we nevertheless say, in Scotland as well as in
Ireland, much that is at present transaoted in
London as Parliamentary business, might be
properly and profitably dealt with away from
there.

Repeal of the Union, however, would not
be likely to benefit either England or Ireland;
whilst separation would, most certainly,
be ruinous to both. To argue this question,
however in reference to the past state of the
two countries in their relation to each other,
would be a waste of time. Faction
in the old days was bad and bitter in every
way. But what the two nations may do by
an honest exercise of popular power for their
mutual welfare, may be, in almost everything,
unlike this. Why should not the masses of
the English people throw their weight into
the scale to help forward all measures cal-
culated to improve the political and social con,

dition of Ireland? Or why should not the
Irish people, reciprocating this spirit, join
themselves in friendliness to their brethren in
England, that the. efforts of each may be pro-
ductive of good in both nations? They have
a strong interest in each other's good—none
whatever in each other's injury. To discover
grounds of agreement—to find out in what
way they can co-operate with each other—to
become convinced that their highest advantage
is to be found in this, is a duty neither should
neglect. The people of Ireland, recovering
from an oppressive nightmare, see in the
present the ugly distortions of the past, and
they fight with departing shadows in a
brighter and clearer present, which they have
not yet had time to understand. They have
not yet realized the growing power of the
people of England, which has nothing in it
inimical to their welfare, but which has many
things in it strongly tending in the direction
of their good. Instead of seeking to out
themselves adrift from England without any
understood principles of political or social
justice upon which to base their intended new
nationality, they should cling to the maturer
thought, and ally themselves to the growing
power of the democracy of England.
The :tipper and middle classes in Ireland
understand less than the same classes in England
or elsewhere the tendency of modern thought,
because those of them who sympathize with
popular struggles, and who, in a certain sense,
guide them, derive their inspiration entirely
from times gone by. They have educated
themselves definitely in memories of the past ;
whilst of hopes connected with the future,
such as animate tho party of action in other
countries, there is no evidence that they are
otherwise than of the vaguest kind. It may
be remarked too, with truth, that their clergy
are only national in name. However they may
be moved temporarily by any immediate influ-
ence; their permanent inspiration has its source
at Rome, and their motives and conduct are
regulated by the policies and ambitions of a
Church rather than by a sense of the require-
ments of the nation. Such priestly advisers as
they have got never yet served in a satisfac-
tory way the purpose of any nation in Europe,
and what has been everywhere discarded as
mischievous is not likely in Ireland to
contradict its history everywhere else.
In their struggles the people of Ireland are
not linked by thought or sympathy with
the oppressed people of any part of
Europe; on the contrary, they seem to have
tied their fate to a party which everywhere
else is hated and warred with by those strug-
gling for the establishment of pelitical and
religious liberty. A cordial union with the
people of• England by the advanced party in
Ireland, were, such a thing possible, would
soon bring about an altered condition of things
in that country. Every step made in advance
would be guaranteed by the united political
strength of the people of both oountries, and
the reign of law—liberal and just law—would
get rid on the one hand of the injustice of the
rich and powerful, and on the other of the evil
adieu of secret conspiracy and the disgraceful
violence growing out of it. A real progress
would set in, and the security given by wise
concert on the part of the people would make
that progress continuous. We are inclined to
say, therefore, that in any attempt that may be
made to reorganize the business of the House
of Commons, one part of the reform should be
the relegation of all Irish local matters to some
native body in Ireland appointed to deal with
them on the spot.

articles.title: ASSASSINATION OF LORD MAYO.
articles.text:
ASSASSINATION OF LORD MAYO.

Tun deplorable death of Lord MAYO excites
universal commisseration. In such a case,
indignation were misapplied. The head man
among the half hundred representatives of
British Sovereignty in different parts of the
EmPiro, falls by the knife of a wretched
hto-
baminedan convict, without either provocation
or motive for the deed. In a thorough spirit
of duty, ho had visited the Great Andaman
Island in the Bay of Bengal, to inspect the
convict colony, and was on the pointof stepping
into the boat which waited to carry him back
to the steamer, when, under cover of dark, the
fanatioalassassin broke through the attendants,
and stabbed hint twice in the back before any

hindrance could be prevented. The wounds
were so deep and mortal that, almost without
uttering a sound, the Governor-General of
India fell down and expired. The attendance
about him was strong enough for protection,
but, in his haste to step aboard, he outwalked
them, and through the opening made, the fatal
blows were struck. The opportunity arose out
the return from work of some two hundred
convicts, and others, of whom the murderer
was one. As the instrument used was a com-
mon dinner knife, the act may have been
without premeditation, and from a sudden
prompting, which the fanatical murderer calls
inspiration of God.
Although Lord MAYO was a Conservative,
and appointed by the Leader of his party, he
had acquired the full confidence of the present
Government, by which he was continued in
office; and, if anything could alleviate to his
widow and family, and, towards the terrible
character of such a bergavement, it would be
such testimonies as were borne to him in the
House of Lords by the Duke of AUGYLL, and
in the House of Commons by Mr. GLADSTONE.
It will be for the Government and the Legisla-
ture not to take unnecessary alarm, but to see
that duo inquiry is made best isolated as this
unhappy act may seem, it should be in any
way connected with that hatred of British
rule, which burst out in the Mutiny, and in
which men of the same race and faith with this
fierce fanatic, bore the most atrocious and most
cruel part.

articles.title: AMERICAN CLAIMS.
articles.text:
THE AMERICAN CLAIMS.

EARL GRANVILLE, the proper, organ of the
Government on all foreign affairs, declines
being drawn out into hasty and premature
declarations on our critical relations with the
United States. Lord REDESDALE put a pair
of questions to him, constructed upon the
hypothetical principle; but the ingenuity of
the constructor became the cause of his defeat.
A. (the Northern States) and B (the Southern
States), being now in partnerBhip, sue C (Eng-
land) for injuries done. But C answers
that, with respect to the whole ground of
complaint, B was acting with him; and,
therefore, the questioner wants to know
whether this fact is not a complete answer to
the suit, and does not render recovery of
damages impossible. In short, Lord REDES-
DALE flattered himself that he had discovered
an unanswerable answer in the circumstance
of the South first doing certain acts, and then,
as partner with the North, who suffered by
them, applying for payment for having done
them.

The analogy thus drawn from the ordinary
law concerning commercial partnerships, must
at least be allowed, to be ingenious. Earl
GITINVII.LE, however, did not feel called upon
, to give an opinion on a point of law, especialy
as raised upon a statement altogether
hypothetical. At any rate, the Governmen t
refer taking one step at a time. li:tor the
present they confine themselves to representing
their view, of the facts, reserving arguments of
whatsoever sort, to a future and proper time.
In both Houses there exists a natural
solicitude for all the information that
Ministers can and feel themselves at liberty to
give; and the PRIME MINISTER has assured
one of the Members for Birmingham, that, as
soon as it will be consistent with duty, the
communication made to the Government at
Washington in consequence of the American
Case, shall be laid before Parliament. Before
this assurance was elicited, Mr. 11XLANDS
had given notice of a resolution (to be moved
on the 12th of March) that, in future, all
treaties between our country and other coun-
tries shall, before ratification, be laid upon the
table of the House, to give it an opportunity of
examining them, and expressing an opinion
on the contents.

On. the 13th instant, President Glum sent
to the Senate a copy of the American Case,
which, as Mr. GLADSTONE has explained in the
House of Commons, had been first, in accord -
anoo with a custom contrary to our own, put
into circulation through the principal Wash-
ington, New York, and other journals. It
thus happens that the American Case was
known to the British public without being
communicated to the Imperial Parliament, be-
cause, as the Parma. showed, the Govern.

'merit could neither communicate officially
what they had not officially received, nor
publish the American Case until prepared to
publish the English also. Now, our usage is not
to put before parliament a doeumen.t on a matter
to be arbitrated upon. Nevertheless, under the
peculiarcircumstances of the ease, the Govern-
ment are disposed to deviate, and will produce
their caso on motion made to that effect. This
intimation is accompanied by the obvious
warning, that we must not read the English
Case with the expectation of any reply to
matter contained in the American Case, be-
cause, of course, the former was prepared
anterior to the reception of the latter, and in
total ignorance of its statements.
In the meantime, we hear from New York,
that the answer to Earl GRANVILLE'S Note
will be on the assumption that, if negotiation
is to continue, the Arbitrators must be allowed
to settle everything put before them on either
side. The New York _Herald maintains its de-
fiant tone; but the Herald isnot even New York,
much less is it all America. Signs of more
importance are not wanting that the demand
for indirect damages will not be persisted in.
The Russians are joining in the bluster, as if
England were sinking into the sea. and the
CzAu and the PRESIDENT were soon to have all
the world to themselves. The American law-
yers sent to argue before the Arbitrators ire
shrewd men; but in
.Paris it is the opinion
of even Americans that the war will be confined
to words, and it may be well imagined that
really shrewd men will not make a very reso-
lute stand on points with respect to which they
have no prospect of winning.

articles.text:
THE BURIALS BILL.

Mr. OSBORNE Mono.or carried the
second reading of his Burials Bill, on last
Wednesday, by a majority of 71. The
opposition of Messrs. BIRLEY, RAINES,
MOWBRAY, and Horn, was strong, not to say
violent. The mover had the support, the very
effective though temperate support of Mr.
HINDE PALMER, as well as of Mr. MORLEY,
and Mr. Mum The last, however, declared
that he took little interest in this question,
except as it branched into another, in which
he tank a very deep interest. The supporters
of the Bill simply claimed a right, they did
not ask a ooncetsion. Churches and church-
yards were not the property of a sect, but of
the nation, and all the Dissenters asked was
the preservation of their rights as citizens in
the national churchyards. Ile thought it far
better that the battle should be fought out on
this principle. The question was, whether
they should consent to be bulled like dogs, or
have what they deemed proper services.
Mr. PALMER promised in Committee to move
clauses which should seoure that the service
performed in the parish churchyards should
be of a sacred and Christian character, and
such as are customarily performed by the
different religious denominations.

Mr. WALIZR made . a quotation from

THE BONAPARTISTS AND THE
OR,LEANISTS.

THE fusion still, hangs fire. While the
Orleans Princes are giving dinners and routs
in Paris, the Count Chambord comes no
nearer than Antwerp. Madame Thiers re-
ceives almost queenly honours at the Duke of
Aumale's, who puts her on the same sofa
with the Countess of Paris. The Bonapartists
point to these things as proofs that M. Thiers
is selling the Republic to the descendants of
his former master. M. Bouher is to take his
seat for Corsica on Monday. M. Conti is
dead, and it remains to be seen whether his
seat will fall to M. Abbatucci who made
room for Rouher, or to M. Clement Duveruois,
These gentlemen give out that they are
coming to defend free trade as well as to
restore the Empire.

articles.text:
THE LATE MR. RICHARD EARN OTT.

THE funeral of Mr. RICHARD HARNOTT, late
Central Corresponding Secretary of the Friendly
Society of Operative Masons, whose death 0C
cured to late for notice in our last, took place at
the Salford Cemetery, Eccles New Road, on
Saturday. afternoon. The circumstances attend-
ing Mr. HARNOTT'S death were of a somewhat
painful character. Up to half-past six en
Tuesday evening, Feb. 6th, he was engaged
in the duties of his office, and: seemed in the
full enjoyment of health. The following
morning, shortly after five o'clock, his wife
awoke to find him lying dead, in bed, his left
side contracted with paralysis.. The funeral
took place from the deceased's residence, ill
Booth-street, West. His remains were accom-
panied to the grave by a large number of
friends and members of the Society. Thc
procession was led by a band, playing
the
"Dead March" in "Sant," succeeded by the
Central Committee and annual Auditors of the
Operative Masons' Society, delegates ffromAltrinoham, Belton, Bradford, Chester, Not-
tingham, and other towns, together with
representatives of the Engineers' Association,
the Amalgamated Carpenters and Joiners', and
the Labohrers' Societies, with a large number
of members of the Society with which the
deceased was connected, making in all about
350 persons; these were followed by the
hearse, drawn by four black horses, behind
which was borne a mason's mallet and chisel
resting on a black velvet cushion. Three
mourning coaches and one private carriage,
bearing the relatives and immediate friends of
the deceased, brought up the rear. The route
was along Booth-street, Medlock-street, Great
Jackson-street, Chester-road, Egerton-street,
Dawson-street, and Regent-road.
By the death of Mr. BARNOTT the operative
masons have lost a faithful friend and
a valued servant. Mr. Hanstorr was born
in Cheshire in 1807, and served his ap-
prenticeship to a stonemason. Twenty-five
years ago he was appointed to the
post he held at the time of his death, aid
throughout
.that time his home has been in
Manchester. He was exceedingly attentivate
his duties, never losing a day. During the
quarter of a century he has been Central Cor-
responding Secretary he has never had a week's
clear relaxation from the duties of his office.
He was much respected, and the news of ills
sudden death has caused amongst mesons
generally, a feeling of sincere grief. 110 Iv°
very exact and conscientious; mild, moderate,
and conciliatory in his disposition; amiable
and courteous in his manners, though some-
what reserved and cautious.

A memoir :of his life would be a history of
the Masons' trnion. To him the masons of
England and Wales are largely indebted for
keeping their Association one and undivided
throughout the length and breadth of the
land. His whole heart and soul was devoted
to his duties; and though his Elalth
visibly failing, no inducement or entreaty on
the part of his friends and official intimates,
could prevail upon him to leave his post. The
Society has wisely, throughout Mr. rail/011'0
term of office, kept to the principle of
re-eligibility of faithful and honest servants.'
He has, for the greater part of his time, had
to submit to an annual contest for his seat, hut
always won by immense majorities. The
Society would do itself credit by adding
principle of re-eligibility to office of faithful
servants, the system of triennial (Anti° lig
instead of annual elections, and an annual
weekly holiday on full pay of its officials.

THE BALLOT BILL.

The Government Bill "to amend the law re-
lating•to procedure at Parliamentary and Munici-
pal Elections" has been printed. It contains 28
clauses, and is divided into three parts. Part I.
relates to Parliamentary elections, and comprises
88 sections, classed as follows :—Procedure at
elections; offences at elections; amendment of the
law; duties of returning and election officers; mis-
cellaneous; application to Scotland; application to
'Part 11. relates to municipal elections,
and comprises four sections. Part 111. contains
mhc,.,llaneous prey:sip:is, chiefly definitions of
terms used. The Schedules are longer than the
Bill. The method is adopted of placing "Rules
for Elections" in a Schedule. The draughtsman,
however; has retained some in the Bill. For in-
stance, the Bill provides in the body of it that
"after the close of the poll" the ballot box shall
be sealed up and taken charge of by the returning
officer, and he in the presence of the candidates'
agents in attendance is to open them and count the
votes given to each candidate and forthwith declare
what candidates are elected. Afterwards the
schedule provides that the returning officer is to
"make arrangements for counting the votes as
soon as practicable after the close of the poll," and
give notice to the agents; and so far as practicable
he is to proceed continuously • with counting the
votes, allowing only time for refreshment, and
excluding (except so far as he and the agents '
otherwise agree) the hours between 7p.m. and 9 a.m.
During the excluded time he is to "take proper
precautions" for the security of the ballot papers,
and place them under his own seal and the soil of
such of the agents *as desire to affix their seals,
The exact details tire obviously of the essence of
the pill, but the following general sketch of the
schema for Parliamentary elections may ba
acceptable :—The' "time appointed for the election"
is to be two hours between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.,

attend" at the place of election' and candidates
may be nominated in writing by two registered

returning officer. The candidates and their pro--
posers and seconders, and no other person (except
to assist the returning officer), will be entitled to

returning officer is to give public notice of the
candidates, and the names of their nominators, and.
of the. order in which the names of the
candidates will be printed in the ballot paper.
The ballot paper is to contain an alphabetical list
of the candidates, with space opposite each name
for the voter to make a mark against the
names of the candidates voted for. A paper of

compartment of) evety polling station. The

"The voter may vote for - candidates.

THE LEAGUE OF PENCE !AND OF
LIRE RTY.-TO THE PEOPLE OF THE
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

We are asked to publish the following
GENEVA, Jan, 6, 1872.
CITIZENS,—,Ono of the vice-presidents of
our League, Mons. Amard Gregg, is about to
go to your country with the intention of
travelling over it, and of interesting it in
our work. We beg of you to accord our
colleague that welcome which his devotion
and the importance of his mission deserve.
Founded at Geneva in 1867, under the
Presidency of General Garibaldi, the League
of Poets° and of Liberty has already held five
Congresses—at Geneva, at Borne, at Basle,
and at Lausanne. During three years it has
published, in French and German, a news-
paper, whose designation "The United States
of Europe" should attract at once your atten-
tion and your sympathies. The late war
suspended its publication. Like all peace
societies we seek the extinction of war; but
the particular character which signalises us
is the idea of founding peace upon political
and social liberty, by instigating the creation
of a Republican Federation of the nations of
Europe. At this very moment your country
gives a grand example of the manner in which
wars may be avoided, by submitting to an
arbitral tribunal the knotty question of the
damages which the Alabama has caused it,
and by choosing, together with England, as
seat of this tribunal, a Swiss town, precisely
that one which was the cradle, and is the
actual seat of our League. Our efforts aim
still further. We would not leave to the
caprice of Governments the task of choosing
or refusing, according to their ambition or
their interests, the eventual path of arbitra-
tion; we would introduce amongst peoples the
means of pada° justice by which differences
are voided among individuals • we would
decide the peoples of Europe first of all, the
most free and the most advanced, to constitute
a federation whiok, without in any way
detracting from the independence or autonomy
of any of the united nations, may spare them
by the creation of a parliament, of an execu-
tive power, of a federal tribunal, and even of
a single federal army, at once interior and ex-
terior security, peace by the means of liberty,
the only one which can become universal and
permanent. This is the labour to which wa
are devoted, without having recourse to other
nuns than discussion and persuasion.
To you citizens, who have for nearly a
century given to the world a practical de-
monstration of the political and moral truths
s
we would implant into old Europe, we come
to demand fraternal aid and support. Aid u
in approximating the day in which, the stars
of the United States of Europe flying freely
by the side of the stars of the United, States of
America, peace shall be &Natively secured
among men.—For the Central Committe,
CH. LEIIONNIER, Vice-President.
T. ROLLANDAY, Secretary and Treasurer.
