articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

At Versaillesa court-martial is trying four-
teen Communist prisoners accused of the
murder of the Dominican monks at Arcueil.
Seventy witnesses are to be heard in the case.

The election in Corsica took place on Sunday.
In Bastia the polling place was guarded by
troops, and two companies of Chasse urs had
been sent into the interior.

In the Prussian Parliament on Saturday,
during the debate on the School Inspection
Bill, Prince Bismarck again complained of the
course adopted by the Roman Catholics in
Germany, who, he said, oared more for the in-
terests of the Church than for those of the
Empire.

A telegram from Rome states that in conse-
quence of the refusal of the King of Spain to
agree to the proposals of the Holy See the
Pope has ordered the tipanish Bishops to
oppose the Government in the forthcoming
elections.

A rumour that Count Bonet had been in-
struoted to return to his post in London in
consequence of the Alabama dispute is con-
tradicted in a Vienna telegram'. The Count
meanwhile has arrived in Venice.

Itis announced from Versailles that in conse-
quence of the Alabama dispute, the attention
of the French Government has been directed to
the necessity of appointing a new Minister at
Washington.

A Berlin Correspondent telegraphs that
public opinion in Germany strongly condemns
the United States for claiming indemnification
for indirect damages.

It is announced from Paris that, after a long
interview with M. Thiers, M. Leon Say, the
Prefect of the Seine, has agreed to withdraw
his resignation.

M. Casimir Perier, it is announced, has de -
elinedthe post of French Ambassador in London
which has been offered to him,

On Saturday the Prince and Princess of
Wales journeyed from Sandringham to Wind-
sor amid the warmest denronstrations of
loyalty. In the last-mentioned town the
reception of their Royal Highnesses was of
the most gratifying character.

The Bishop of London has addressed a
letter to the Association of Lay Helpers in his
diocese. His Lordship, while seeing many
evidences of the value of this organization,
points out that classes in the metropolis are
locally as well as socially divided, and that
efforts to aid the ignorant, the poor, and the
thriftless are "most wanting where they are
most wanted." The right rev. prelate makes
an earnest appeal to those who live in districts
where no .great want exists, on behalf of
those poor and populous neighbourhoods
where the need is the greater, and where
there are few or none to help.

Archbishop Manning's Lenten Pastoral was
read on Sunday in all the Roman Catholic
places of worship in the diocese of Westminster.
The late changes in the statute law in respect
to the Universities have, the Archbishop con-
tends, effaced Christianity from the higher
culture of our youth, and prepared the way for a
harvest of scepticism and unbelief. Dr.
Manning maintains that the doctrines of
Catholic faith and morals demonstrate and
bind the consciences of his co-religionists to
the two following principles; first, that the
schools of Christian people cannot he separated
without sin from the Christian Church; and
secondly, that the education of a Christian
people does not and cannot belong to the juris-
diction of the civil power. It was argued at
length by the Archbishop, that Englafid had a
political right to Anglican, Scotland to
Presbyterian, and Ireland had every right
to Catholic education. The attempt to set
up an uniform, universal, compulsory,
and secular education for these king-
doms would be to inaugurate an age of the
worst despotism over the consciences of a
Christian people. The people of these king-
doms would never permit the consciences of
parents to be violated, or allow their rights
over the training and formation of their off-
spring to be taken from them by a Platonic
Republic or by a Parisian Commune.

A: stringent dockyard order has been issued
by the Admiralty with reference to the future
survey and inspection of ships, and apportion-
ing amongst various officials the responsibility
for the vessels being in all respects fit for the
service whieh they may be required to per-
form.

On behalf of Captain Trench a petition has
been lodged against the return of Captain
Nolan for the county Galway. Intimidaticin
by mobs and by the Homan Catholic priesthOod
is alleged.

r On Saturday evening the Earl of Kimberley
took the chair at a complimentary banquet to
the Hon. G. F. Verdon, who for many years
has acted as agent-general in this country for
the colony of 'Victoria. The Duke of Edin-
burgh, in acknowledging one of the loyal
toasts, spoke of the sympathy which had been
manifested throughout the empire for the
Prince of Wales during the dangerous illness
of his Royal Highness, and testified to its
appreciation by every member of the Royal
Family. Lord Kimberley, in the course of
the evening, described our colonies as being
generally prosperous, adding that the convic-
tion of the English people undoubtedly was
Hint everything possible should be done to
maintain the existing union between our
distant possessions and the mother country.
If, however, a separation must come, he
trusted it might be effected without any
disturbance of friendly relations. Honours
from the Orders of St. Michael and St. George
and of the Bath have been conferred upon
Mr. Verdon by her Majesty.

In speaking at a Volunteer dinner at
Willis's Booms on Saturday evening, the
Duke of Cambridge made some pointed obser-
vations on the Easter Monday review. Going to
Brighton was an excellent thing if it was
understood that it was merely a military pro-
menade, an amusement, an opportunity of
getting together a largo body of Volunteers,
to show their existence, to show that their ap-
pearance was good, and that they could turn
out strong. Butit was utterly and physically
impossible to gain any military knowledge.
If there were no march past more might be
done in the way of evolutions, but, with the
best feeling towards the Volunteers, he must
say that the time hitherto at their disposal for
these displays was too short to allow them to
do well that which they had hitherto at-
tempted.

In the Upper House of Convocation on
Saturday, an address to the Queen was
adopted, thanking her Majesty for the gracious
reference to the late Bishop Patteson in the
Royal Message read at the opening of Parlia-
ment, and • praying that measures might be
taken to put down "the traffic in the bodies
of men" which has sprung up in those dis-
tant islands. In the Lower House the ex-
pediency of adopting a shortened form of daily
service in parish churches was the principal
topics of discussion.

During Sunday the tides on the Thames
rose to a treat height, overflowing the banks
in all the low-lying districts, and causing
considerable damage to house and other pro-
perty. The thoroughfares in many parts were
under water, and in view of a greater over-
flow, the inhabitants of houses situated on the
banks of the river °reefed dams to keep the
water from finding its way into the cellars.

The Paris Constitution says —" The Ala-
bama question, as the English papers call it,
seems likely to assume an ugly look for Great
Britain. We have already mentioned the pre-
tensions of the Amerieans ; they are exorbitant,
and it is impossible to admit that the Cabinet
of Washington can have seriously thought
of claiming an indemnity of from four to five
milliards, without being ready to accept all
the consequences of the certain refusal of
Great Britain. . . . There is no doubt
that the British Government would never have
ratified the Convention of Washington and
accepted the principle of arbitration, if the
Washington Cabinet had clearly manifested
its intention of including in its account the
indirect losses' of the Union. Yet the text
of the Convention authorises to a certain
point the American interpretation; reference
is made to damages resulting from the acts of
°Alija ships,' without any exact limitation
of the extent of those consequences."

A meeting has been held in Bristol in favour
of the extension of the franchise to women,
and resolutions were passed approving of
legislation to that effect. Lady Amberley,
presided, and among the other speakers were
Lord Amberley, Miss Sturge, of Birmingham,
and Miss Ashworth, of Bath.

On Monday morning the Earl of Moray was
found dead in the room where he had break-
fasted, at Darnaway Castle, near For'res:
Apoplexy had been the cause of dphth. The
deceased nobleman, who was '132 years of age,
.3 succeeded in the title im'cl egtfite§ by his
only surviving brother, the lion. George
Stuart.

Mr. Sheriff Bennett was on Monday elected
without opposition to the seat on the London
School Board for the district of the City, vacant
through the resignation of the Rev. W. Rogers.

A Paris correspondent says that the pro-
motet's of the proposed reintroduction of public
gambling in France speak tnost confidently of
sucoess. According to the Gnuicis it hal
already been decided in prinaiple that the
gaming-table shall be established in certain
places; and the Figaro says that the subject
Is shortly to be brought before the French
Assembly, , , ,

The return of John Ruskin, LL.D., as
Rector for the University of St. A,ndrew's
was, it will be remembered, challenged by the
Conservative students on the ground that his
election was illegal, the Scottish University
, Act, 21 and 22 Vic., precluding any principal
or professor of any university from being eli-
gible for the office of rector. The senators of
the university lately submitted a memorial to
eminent counsel on this point. The opinion
which has just been received states that
although the Ad was evidently framed to
exclude only Scottish professors, yet, from the
wording of the clause, Mr. Ruskin being a
professor at Oxford, cannot hold the office of
rector. Counsel also states that the office
falls to the other candidate, Lord Lytton, he
(according to the Act) being the only eligible
candidate of the two. Whether Lord Lytton
will accept the honour now is thought doubt-
ful. St. Andrew's University is thus placed
in rather peculiar circumstances, the court
having neither a rector nor,tt rector's assessor,
and, being thus incomplete, business is at a
standstill.

The Edinburgh University authorities have
been making inquiries into the disturbance
during the address of Sir W. Stirling Maxwell
on the occasion of his installation as Rector
of the University. One of the students has
been rusticated, and several have been fined
and put on probation during the remainder of
their college career. It is said that some of
the ringleaders in the disturbance were not
connected with the University at all, but were
persons who had obtained admission by falsely
representing themselves to be students.

Lord Hominy on Monday gave judgment in
the suit of Gilchrist v. Herbert, argued a
short tune ago. It was brought by a lady,
who claimed one-half of the property of her
late husband, by virtue of an alleged promise
made by him in a letter written to her before
the marriage. At that time Gilchrist was a
widower, and the plaintiff a widow, each with
issue by the previous marriage; and it was
contended by Gilehrist's daughter, who had
inherited the whole of her father's property,
that he could not have made such a promise
to his second wife. The Master of the Rolls,
however, came to the conclusion that the
plaintiff had established her ease.

In the Court of Exchequer on Monday, the
clerk of the S. Pancras Vestry recovered
£1,500 as compensation for injuries received
upon the North London Railway.

At the last meeting of the Court of Common
Council, Mr. Nelson, the City Solicitor, re-
ported that the Corporation of London had
been summonod to the Bow-street Police- court
by the Board of Inland Revenue for not having
taken out a licence for its armorial bearings,
and stated that from 1798, when the tax was
first imposed, down to the present time, no such
payment had ever Seen demanded of or paid
by the Corporation. -The summons had been
issued without any communication, formal or
otherwise, with the City authorities, and it
would come on for hearing within a week.
The Court, with many expressions of astonish-
ment on the matter, left it to the City solicitor
to defend the summons on behalf of the cor-
poration.

Vice-Chancellor Wickens gave judgment on
Saturday upon the general demurrer to the
bill filed by Mr. Hepworth Dixon against the ,
printer and publisher of the _Pall 3J91.
Gazette. Mr. Dixon alleged that in certain
numbers of the paper referred to he had been
libelled, and that he was desirous of learning
the names of the proprietors, to enable him to
take proceedings at law against them. The
defendant's solicitor declined to furnish the
names, and the plaintiff accordingly filed a
bill in Chancery to compel the defendant to
supply such information as was necessary to
the prosecution of the action. His Honour
overruled the demurrer to this bill.

The official correspondence which took place
respecting the elevation of Sir It. P. Collier to
the Judicial Bench was issued on Saturday. To
the letters which previously appeared are now
added those of Chief Justice Bovill and Mr.
Justice Willes. The former concurred with
the views expressed by Sir Alexander Cock-
burn, but Justice Willes was of opinion that
the appointment was legal, and within the
terms of the statute.

Intelligence reaches us from Washington
that a copy of the American Casehas been sent
to the Senate by President Grant, and that the
Mixed Commission has adjourned until the
20th of next month. The Netv York Herald
seems to have heard that Great Britain has
proposed to settle the Alabama claims by a sum
down, and it accordingly announces that it is
now too late for such an arrangement, as Ame-
rica cannot recede from the position she has
takon up.

A. special telegram from our Paris corres-
pondent announces that M. Rouher, the Bona-
partist who has just been returned for Corsica,
will not take his seat in the Assembly until
Monday next. The death of M. Conti, for-
merly Secretary of the Emperor Napoleon,
creates another vacancy in Corsica. It is said
that M. Clement Duvernois, the well-known
Imperialist, is likely to be a candidate for the
seat.

At the Versailles Court-martial which is try-
ing the prisoners charged with the murder of the
Dominicans at Arcueil, General Chanzy gave
evidence on Wednesday in favour of Serizier,
one of the accused. General Chanzy said that
when he and a deputy were made prisoners on
March 19, 1871, and about to be shot by the
mob, Serizier interposed, displayed much cou-
rage and good feeling, and saved their lives.

The trial of Blanqui, celebrated conspirator,
commenced on Thursday before a Court-mar-
tial at Versailles. He is accused in the in-
dictment of having taken part on the 31st
October, 1870, in an attempt to excite the
citizens of Paris to civil war, and of having
arrested and detained the members of the
Government of National Defence.

The Paddington Vestry has resolved to
water their roads with patent salts during the
next twelve months.

Goodall, the huntsman of Mr. Tailby's
country, has reoeived the appointment of
huntsmau to tho Queen's Staghounds.

The S. George's, Hanover-square, Union
Board of Guardians have decided to send
thirty more children out to Canada in charge
of Miss Rye, and to request her to furnish
every six months the addresses of all the
children belonging to the Union whom she
had taken out with her.

Mr. John Poole, a literary man well known
half a century ago, died in the Kentish-town-
road on Monday week. His claim to reputa-
tion rests principally on his comedy of "Paul
Pry," which was produced in 1825, with Mr.
Liston in the character of the hero. Mr.
Poole, who was uoarly eighty years of ago,
Was long in receipt of a pension from the
Civil List. '

A terrifie explosion took place on Friday at
on iron foundry near Merthyr Tydvil, by
which one person was killed on the spot and
others severely injured. The building was
completely shattered, and gigantic iron beams
Were snapped like rods. During a casting the
mould broke, and the molten metal, coming
in contact with the surrounding water,
caused the accident.

Mr. Bent, late inspector of factories, and
father of the Road murderess, died on
Tuesday Week, at Ruthin, North Wales, and
•has been interred in Llangollen churchyard
by the side of his late wife, mother of the
murdered child.

The death at an advanced age is announced
of William Harrison, the " Fon Poet," of the
Isle of Ely. He was I'r forty years the
superintendent of the Burnt Fen district, and
only retired a few years ago on a pension.

Anthony Scott, aged thirty-seven years, a
labourer employed at Mr. Martineau's sugar
works, destroyed himself by poison after being
dismissed for taking twopennyworth of sugar.
He took cyanide of potassium in presence of
his wife, who was ill in bed dying. He could
not boar the stigma of 4; thief " on his name,
and in a letter connnended his wife and chil-
dren to the consideration of his employers.

At Chipping Norton, one of Messrs. Bliss's
tweed factories was entirely consumed on
Wednesday. The fire was visible at Oxford,
a distance of twenty miles, and the damage
done is put at £70,000, besides throwing out
numerous bands.

Edward S. Stokes, the murderer of James
Fisk, has been arraigned 'for trial in New
York. His counsel. who are leading New
York criminal lawyers, will fight the case at
every step, and accordingly they began with a
motion to quash the indictment.

A crowded meeting was held on Tuesday
night in the Agricultural 'Hall, Wolverhanip-
ton, to support the legalization of marriage with
a deceased wife's sister. Resolutions were
rpssed unanimously, and a petition to both
outics of Parliatiieht iitas adopted. .

An action to recover damages for breach of
promise of marriage was tried on Monday in the
Bail Court, in which the plaintiff was a domestic
servant, while the defendant carried on the
business of ft brewer and licensed victualler.
The jury returned a verdict for the plainti
damages, £250.

A shocking crime has been committed in
India. Lord Mayo, the Governor-General,
has been assassinated by a convict in the
Andaman Islands. The melancholy news was
announced on Monday night in both Houses
of Parliament, in the Lords by the Duke of
Argyll, and in the Commons by Mr. Glad-
stone. It seems that Lord Mayo was on his
way to Rangoon when the tragic event
occurred. His assassin, a Mahommedan
fanatic, under sentence of imprisonment for
life for murder, stabbed his lordship twice
in the back, the guards in attendance being
taken by surprise. It was dusk at the time.
The murder took place at the convict settle-
ment of Fort Blair, and was committed on
Thursday, just as Lord Mayo had concluded his
inspection of the station, and was about to
embark on board the man-of-war; but, owing
to the absence of telegraphic communication
with the main land, the news did not reaoh
this country until Monday afternoon. Lord
Mayo was born in 1822, and succeeded his
father in 186'i as sixth earl in the peerage of
Ireland. He was appointed Governor-General
of India in 1868 by Mr. Disraeli, having
previously acted as Chief Secretary for
Ireland. Ile married, in 1858, a daughter of
the first Baron Lecontield, and leaves four
sons and two daughters. The eldest son is an
officer in the 10th Hussars.

A special telegram contains additional par-
ticulars respecting the assassination of Lord
Mayo. The Viceroy had complained more
than once of the precautions taken, and as he
was about to proceed to his boat, he quickened
his pace, and the armed guard which attended
him became less compact. At that moment
the assassin, who had previously been unno-
ticed, milled forward, and committed the
crime. He declares that he was inspired by
God. Lord Mayo died a few minutes after he
was struck down. The murderer belongs, it
seems, to the Hill tribes of the laybz...r Pass.
His weapon was an ordinary table-knife, and
either of the two wounds inflicted by it was
sufficient, it is said, to have caused death.
He was at once arrested, and his trial was
proceeding when the steamer left the island.
Intense excitement was caused in Bombay by
the news of the assassination, and in Calcutta
all business was suspended. Mr. John
Strachey, a member of the Indian Govern-
ment, is acting for the present as Viceroy, as
Lord Napier of Merehiston, the Governor of
Madras, wishes to take his seat in the Council
before assuming the office which has devolved
upon him.

We learn from Washington that Mr. Sum-
ner has proposed. that a Committee of the
Senate shall institute an inquiry for the pur-
pose of ascertaining whether the sale of Go-
vernment arms and ordnance stores to France
during the late war was a violation of the
neutrality of the United States.

A Rome telegram states that the Italian Go-
vernment has been assured by General Sherman
that the American Government hopes the
Alabama question will be peacefully and
definitely settled by the Geneva arbitrators.

In the Prussian Parliament the Bill on the
inspection of primary schools was passed by
207 to 155 votes. Prince Bismarck, in the
course of the debate, denied that he had pre-
viously accused the Catholic Church in Ger-
many of being anti-national, but maintained
that the clergy, acting as inspectors of schools,
had tried to obstruct the teaching of the Ger-
man language, and had openly declared that
they could only be saved by the French.

Last week the aggregate mortality in Lon-
don and twenty other large towns in the
United Kingdom was at the rate of 27 deaths
annually to every 1,000 persons estimated to
be living. lathe metropolis 2,492 births and
.1,524 deaths were registered, the former
having been one above, and the latter 121
below, the average. Sixty-eight persons died
from small-pox, 40 from measles, 31 from
scarlet fever,' 3 from diphtheria, 88 from
whooping-cough, 27 from different forms of
fever (of which four were certified as typhus,
15 as enteric or typhoid,, and 8 as simple con-
tinued fever)) and 13 from diarrhma. The
temperature agaiu showed a remarkable
excess; the mean of the week was more than
46 degrees, or eight above the average for the
same week in fifty years. The average daily
excess during the 60 days ending Saturday
last was 4.6. The 480 deaths from diseases
of the respiratory organs 'showed a further
slight decline upon the numbers in recent
weeks.

M:Roulter, the:well-known Bonapartist, has
been returned for Corsica by a large majority.
There were two other eamliclates-3f. SaveHi,
an advanced ,Republican and Count Pozzo di
Berg°.

The Mormon trials are postponed until
March, in consequence of the United States
Attorney-General having no appropriation
from Congress to meet the expenses, and the
territorial authorities refusing to pay them.

We hear that the Rev. M. J. J. Variner, of
Patna, whose name has frequently appeared
lately in the journals in connection with ex-
periments in producing wines and brandies
from the jamun and other fruits, have been
removed from the roll of missionaries of the
Society for the Propagation of the Gospel.

Prince Arthur has accepted the presidency
of the Victoria Park Hospital, the foundation-
stone of which was laid by the late Prince
Consort. His Royal Highness has consented
to preside at the anniversary dinner of St.
John's Foundation School for Poor Clergy in
April.

The Earl of Carnarvon arrived in town on
Wednesday, but is still too unwell to attend
to his Parliamentary duties.

Prince Charles Bonaparte, who has lately
arrived from Rome, has spent a night in
visiting the slums of Shoreditoh, Ratcliffe
Highway, &c. He was escorted by Mr. B.
Jerrold, and a detective policeman.

Captain Dimond, of the ship Naomi, which
has just arrived in the Mersey from Maccio,
reports that from January 30, when off the
Western Islands, the vessel encountered strong
gales from S.W. to N.N.W. up to the chops of
the Channel, and from thence strong breezes
from S. to S.E. On the 3rd of February the
Naomi fell in with great quantities of cocoa
nuts, and on the following day passed three
dead bodies, apparently seamen, having on
their sea boots; also several sou'-westers float-
ing about. There was a very heavy sea
running at the time, and the wind was blow -
ings strong from the S.S.E.

It has been ascertained that Mr. Bauer,
the Russian gentleman who disappeared so
, mysteriously on the 26th ult., had an interview
on the morning of that day with an official
of the Society of Arts in the Adelphi Hotel,
London. He also had an interview, at the
Charing-cross Hotel, with Mr. Leslie, the
manager of the Moscow Gas Works, He left
that hotel shortly after 11 and drove in a cab
to Eaton station, where he arrived at 11.40
twenty minutes before the train started for
Birmingham. This fact has been ascertained
from the cabman who drove Mr. Bauer to the
station. The porter who took charge of Mr.
Bauer's portmanteau states that be (Bauer)
said he would wait for the next train, which
left at 3 p.m. He afterwards went to the
telegraph office, and at five minutes past. 12'
telegraphed to Birmingham announcing that
he had missed the train. Au expert has
declared that the two letters, the one signed
by Tht.uer and the other by "A Sufficient
Number," had been written by one man.

On Thursday a meeting of the Society for
the Repression of Mendicity was held to con-
sider a report on the best means of effecting
that object throughout the country, Mr. A.
Johnston, M.P., presiding. After much dis-
cussion, a resolution was passed, declaring
that the adoption of a uniform system was
essential to the carrying out of the purpose
contemplated by the organisation. Another
resolution advocated the strict enforcement of
the ,vagrancy laws. The meeting was then
adjourned to this day.

The remains of the late Mr. John Foreman,
the well-known head of one of the Baptist
Denominations, were on Thursday interred in
Kensal-green Cemetery.

The name of his Majesty the King of S'am
is as follows :—Pra Bat Somdeteh Prabaramain
Taramaha Chttlalonkorn Klao Pra Chao Pen
Din Siam.

The half-yearly meeting of the Metropolitan
Railway Company was held on Thursday.
Some dissatisfaction was expressed at the
amount of the dividend, and an amendment
appointing a committee of investigation was
negatived by only a narrow majority. A poll
was demanded, but it was not pressed, on the
ehairman's offer to aecept, as additions to the
board, two gentlemen named by the proprie-
tors.

From Bombay we learn that in consequence
of the assassination the ceremonies connected
with the unveiling of statues of the Queen and
the late Prince Consort have been postponed.

At a meeting of the Geographical Society on
Monday, Sir Henry RawHugon, the president,
Stated that the expedition 'in search of Dr.
Livingstone had started three days ago, ac-
companied by Lieuts. H. Dawson, R.N. and
Donald Livingstone, the sou .Of the great
traveller. The fund raised for the expedition
amounted to £5,000, £2,600 of which had
been subscribed in London, and X2OO had
been raised in the little Scotch town of Hamil-
ton, the birthplace of Dr. Livingstone.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.
The French Government will probably present
to the Assembly a Bill fixing New Caledonia
as the place of transportation for the con-
demned Communist prisoners.
The delegates of the Right have left for
Antwerp to submit their programme of a
Monarchical fusion to the Count de Clam-,
bord. The Right Centre, though approving
the programme, are not inclined to sign it.
The Count de Chambord, it is reported, will
also refuse to accept it.

In accordance with orders from the Chief
Commander of the Russian Fleet, 25 vessels
are being prepared and armed in the Black Sea
to take part in the naval manosuvres next
summer.

An inquest was opened Yesterday on Thomas
Bradshaw, watchman at the Alexandra Theft.
tre, Sheffield, who committed suicide by hang-
ing himself amid the " cloud scenes,,' thirty
feet above the stage. He had previously bat-
toted his wife's head with a poker until she
was unconscious, and probably left her for
dead. It was stated that she could not sur-
vive, and the inquest was adjourned.
, Mr. Partridge, at the Southwark Police-
court, yesterdaay, after hearing two representa-
tive oases outof the forty raised by the Lambeth
Vestry against the oostermongers, said he must
administer the law as he found it; and the
defendants, having created an obstruction and
a nuisance, must be fined in the mitigated
penalty of ss. each and costs. Mr. Partridge
said a good word for the vestry, which had
offered a compromise in point of time; and a
significant word for the shopkeepers in draw-
ing the attention of the police to an IA of last
session, enabling them to proceed against "the
tradesmen who carried on their bustnese at the
same time as the oostormongers."
The late Huxley and Cromer Election
Committee unanimously, resolved that Mr.
Cremer be put forward as a candidate for
the seat at the London School Board shortly
to be vacant by the resignation of Professor
Huxley.

His Royal Ilighness the Duke of Edinburgh
left the Victoria Station yesterday morning
for Portsmouth on his way to Osborne.

The Comte de Chambord has arrived nt
Antwerp, where he intends residing.
The Pain's states that the police arc search-
ing Paris for concealed arms.

In yesterday's sitting of the National
Assembly the committee presented their report
•on the Government Bill according pensions to
the widows of General Clement Thomas, and
M. Chaudey. The committee propose that a
pension should be given to the widow of the
former only, and this amended proposal wan
read a first time.

At Manchester, yesterday morning, Andrew
Macbeth, late cashier at the Manchester and
County Bank, was committed for trial, charged
with embezzling £1,200, belonging to his
employer. When apprehended he confessed
that he had taken the money, and that his
defalcations had extended over some years.

THE POLICE AND PUBLIC MEETINGS.

Mr. Bruce ha s• received
.tx deputation of
gentlemen of various political parties who
wished to urge the necessity of making an
alteration in the present pollee regulations
with respect to the maintenance of order at
public meetings. Among those who formed
the deputation were Lord W. P. Lennox,
Lord Alfred Churchill, Sir Henry Hoare, M.P.,
Mr. Raikes, M.P., Sir Alfred Slade, Sir James
Sibbald Scott, and Captain Charles Mercier.
The deputation described the disgraceful and
riotous interruption to public meetings which
had lately taken place in Chelsea, and suggested
that the police should be ordered to protect
, the peace at public) irThetings which may be
assembled for a lawful objeoti whether they
' are called upon to do so or not; and that the
conveners of any publio meeting who may
have reason to anticipate a breach of the pane°
should, by giving notice in writing at the
Home-office of the meeting and of its ohjeet,
be entitled to police protection, provided the
object of the meeting appear to the Homo Sec-
retary to be a lawful one. Mr. Bruce said he
should see with groat regret any interference
with the freedom of public meetings. Hitherto
there had in this country been sufficient re-
spect for the views of others to make it unne-
cessary that the freedom of public speech
should be guarded by the police. The police
were already empowered to enter a public
meeting if called upon to suppress an actual'
breach of the peace, or to take into eustddy
any person charged with committing an offence
of which the police can take legal cognisance,
and he declined to undertake at present to make
any alterations in a rule which had worked
well since the foundation of the police force.
If, however, such serious
,disturbances as had
been referred to continued, it might become
necessary to alter the present regulations

TIVERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.-FRIDAY.

The House of Lords sat for twenty minutes.
The business was of a formal nature.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.7-.FninAr.

The Commons was occupied with the elec-
tion of a Speaker in the place of Mr. Denison,
who retires.

There was no opposition to Mr. Brand, who
was proposed by Sir Roundeli Palmer and
seconded by Mr. Locke King.
In placing his services at the disposal of the
House, Mr. Brand said he should always look
for his guidance to the rules and orders of the
House, and for his examplo to the long roll of
distinguished men who had preeeded him in
office.

Mr. Brand having been formally conducted
to the chair, Mr. Gladstone assured the Right
Hon. Gentleman that ho received the full con-
fidence and approbation of the House.
The House then adjourned until Monday.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY.

In the House of Lords the new tapeaker of
the House of Commons was officially received
by Her Majesty's Commissioners.
The Duke of Argyll read a telegram from
Mr. Ellice, a member of the Council of India,
announcing that on the Bth instant, the Earl
of Mayo, the Viceroy of India, was assassinated
in one of the Andernan Islands, by a Mahom-
medan convict. The noble Duke on the part
of Her Majesty's Government, expressed deep
sympathy with the family of Lord. Mayo, and
Mid the conduct of his Lordship as Governor-
General, fully:justified the choice made of him
by the :late Government. He added that he
was afraid that Lord Mayo had fallen a victim
to the almost excessive discharge of his public
duties, for if he had a failing it was that he
would leave nothing to others but desired
to see everything for himself. •
The Duke :of Richmond in referring to the
sad news, briefly added his testimony to :the,
loss the country .had sustained in the death of
Lord Mayo. .
. Lord Lifford called attention to the working
of the Irish Lind Act, and moved for returns
of the land cases decided in the counties of
Antrim and Donegal.
The Earl of Duffcrin, on the part of the
Government, assented to the motion which was
agreed to, _

On the motion of Earl Beauchamp, the
Ilurial Grounds Bill was read a second time.
The Union of BoneficeE Bill was read a first
titne. Their Lordships then adjourned.'
'HOUSE OF COMMONS.--MoNiut.

In the House of Commons on Monday, the
Speaker-eleet took his seat at four o'clock, and
was shortly afterwards summoned to the
House of Lords. On his return the Speaker
took the chair, and almost immediately rose
arid announced to the House that he had been
to the House of Lords, end that the Lords
authorised by ,!Ifor Majesty's Commission had
declared that Her Majesty had been pleased to
approve of the choice the House of Commons
had made of him as their Speaker.
Mr. Gladstoiae made an announcement in
similar terms to that made in the Upper Rouse
respecting the assassination of the Earl of
Mayo, Her Majesty's Viceroy in India, and
spoke in the highest terms of the ability aud
devotion of his lordship to tho public service.
Mr. Disraeli expressed his deep regret at the
sudden calamity, which, he said, overwhelmed
him as one of the private friends of the unfor-
tunate nobleman. Colonel Sykes expressed
his belief that the deplorable act was one of
private malice and not of political significance.
In reply to a question, Mr. Gladstone said
he must draw a distinction between the Eng-
lish and American Cases. The latter had been
printed for the use of Congress, but as it had
not been published in America, it would not
be right to publish it here. As regarded the
English Case, it was prepared for a special pur-
pose to lay before the Tribunal, and as soon
as that purpose was a little more advanced,
there would be no objection to give it.
In reply to Mr. 'Tapp)? Bright, Mr. Bruce said
a bill for the amondffient of the Truck Act
would be introduced on the first possible oppor-
tunity.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer briefly de-
fended the Treasury in the matter of withhold-
ing aid to the expedition about to be sent.oixt
in search of Dr. Livingstone, and explained
that it was not desirable that the Government
should join in private subscriptions for which
Parliament in its wisdom had placed no funds
at its disposal.
On the motion of Mr. , Ayrton, the Royal
Parks and Gardens Bill was read a second
time.

• Mr. Bruce, in moving for leave to introduce
a bill to consolidate and amend. the Acts re-
lating to the regulation of alinesp expressed his
regret at the matter having been so long in
hand. Having brouglit the bill before the
House before, he would not enter into detail,
beyond explaining the changes which he pi 0-
posed to introduce into the bill this year. The
bill of last year applied to coal and ironstone
raines, and was now extended to stratified iron
mines, &c. With regard to the employment
of boys, the provisions w..re the same is those
of lust year so far Eid practical, the prin.
woo of the notory Act would be tipplied;

The question of wages was not dealt with, in
consequence of the Government being about to
deal with that question in a bill to amend the
Truck Act. One important alteration will be
propositions to establish, as far as possible, a
uniform rate of weighing at the pit mouth ;
but power would bo :given the Secretary of
State, on the 'report of an inspector, to adopt a
certain amount, though this would only be
done in very exceptional circumstances. With
regard to double shafts, he proposed that there
should be a communication between them of
4ft. wide and 3ft. high. Public attention had
recently been called to the loss of life by acci-
dents in mines, but only about one-fourth of
these occurrences arose from explosions: What
he thought was urgently needed was the- want
of vigorous discipline, and he, therefore, pro-
posed that a manager should be appointed
by each mine owner. At present the law gave
very little security so far as managers were
concerned, but yet, of all officers, he was the
most important. It was now propesedthat all
managers .appointed since: 'January, 1872,
should pass an examination, and should re-
ceive a certificate of his fitness. In the event
of any striorta charge being brought against
him, it should be the duty of :the Secretary of
State to institute an inquiry into those charges.
One of the new provisions of the bill was that
the owners should be held responsible for the
roofs and sidings. No gunpowder should be
used, except in cartridges, and on no account
should it be used for blasting, except in blast-
ing mines, and then only liva person who shall
be held responsible. Another provision of the
hill was that persons employed in a mine might
from time to time appoint two•of their number
to inspect the mine at their own cost, and once
at least in every month the whole mine and
workings should be open to their inspection,
in order that they might be satisfied as to their
safety. This plan had been adopted with sue..
cess in: his own locality, and ho thought it was
a plan which might be adopted' with great acb-
vantage. With regard to 'ventilation, various
plans had been from time to time suggested,
and it was intended to leave the subject in
this way.. The employer must show that the
ordinary state of the intne was one which pro-
vided sufficient ventilation, and that would be,
if shown, a sufficient defence, and no court
would have the power to convict him. It
would be, of course, assumed that where the
general ventilation was sufficient, any accident
me
which might occur must be due to so tem-
porary disarrangement of the workings' over
which the owner had no control. All colliers
were subject to temporary derangements which
were not under the 'control of the masters, and
ho thought this bill would effectually meet the
case.. Then, as to inspections, he considered
that the present number of twelve inspectors
was Utterly insufficient to inspect the mines in
a similar way to factories. It had
,been do-
sired that the mines ' should be inspected at
least once every quarter, and that reports
'should be presented to a responsible Minister,
who should be appointed and called the Minis-
ter of Mines, and whose :duty it should be to
consider the reports of the inspectors, and
'would entirely control all mining operations.
It was, however, utterly impossible this could
be done, and he believed if the plan was adopted
it would be opposed to the interest of the
men thetnselves. What was wanted: was con-
stant, vigilant, and early and even hourly in-
spection, by those most interested, namely,
the men, their agents, and the 'masters. The
bill he now introduced increased the responsi-
bility of the owners, created managers who
were now and responsible officers,' and whose
future career depended upon the vigilance with
which he discharged his duties. Then, as he
had before 'said, the men 'could appoint some
of their own body to inspect the mines, and he
belie*ed such self-acting machinery would be
infinitely better than any other :that could be
devised.

FEB. 17, 18123

'THE NATIONAL -TIILNtSGIVING.

-It is now regarded as definitively settled that
the Royal procession will return from the
Cathedral' by the Embankment route where
the vestrymen of the metropolis will have a
Place allotted to them. On Thursday at the
meeting of the St. Pancras Vestry, it was an-
nounced amidst considerable applause that the
Metropolitmi Board of Works had resolved to
provide aceomodation on the Thames Embank-
ment for every vestryman in the metropolis;
two tickets would be sent to every member.
'Though no official programme is yet in
existence, it is probable that the details of the
procession and Thanksgiving will be comewhat
as follows. Her Majesty will start from Buck,
ingham Palace, through Pall Mall, Charing-
cross, Strand, Fleet-street, and Ludgate-hill.
At Temple-bar the Lord Mayor, Sheriffs, and
a deputation of Aldermen and members of the
Common 'Council will deliver to Her Majesty
the City sword and receive it back, according
to ancient custom. The Lord Mayor, Sheriffs
and the deputation will precede Her Majesty
to St. Paul's in their carriages, and the Queen
will be received at the great west door of the
Cathedral by the Bishop of London, the Dean
and Chapter. of the Cathedral, and certain
High Officers of State, who will conduct Her
Majesty to the Royal pew, nearly in the centre
.of the dome area. 'The new organ of the
Cathedral will play tintil the Queen has taken
her seat. There is every probability that the
Prince of Wales will himself be present at the
Thanksgiving with the Princess, and, it is be-
lieved, their Royal Highnesses' . children. A
guard of honour will be posted at the west
entrance; the Yeomen of the Guard will be
on duty in the Cathedral; the streets and
park will be kept by troops, and in St. James's
Park and the Tower guns will be fired at the
conclusion of the service. The Diplomatic
Body, Distinguished Foreigners, High Sheriffs
of Counties, Mayors, and a representative
selection from the Church, the Army, the
Navy, the Bar, and the Civil Service will be
among those who will. receive official invita-
tions. Her Majesty will go to the Cathedral
not in State, but in semi-State. The Officers
of the -Household will appear in levee dress,
but the ladies in morning dress.

The shops along the route are full of pla-
cards of windows to let, workmen are putting
Up seats at the Church of St. Mary, and the
London, Chatham, and Dover Railway
Company are painting their bridge a neutral
colour. As to the general decoration of the
Strand and Ludgate-hill, nothing seems quite
decided, though there is a talk of Ezeoutive
Committees taking the matter in hand. The
City Architect, it is said, has been ordered to
prepare a design for the decoration of Temple
Bar, a praiseworthy though somewhat modest
step in the right direction. Inside the Cathe-
dral the galleries begin to rise, and to judge
by their ponderous timbers they are being
strongly constructed. That in the North
Transept is to be three-tiered. Negoeiations
are in progress to enable the Charity Children
to take advantige of these galleries and to
hold their festival a. few days after the
Thanksgiving.

A letter from Rome says that the statement
that Anton°lli has denounced the Concordat
of 1801, relative to Alsace and Lorraine, is
incorrect.
